Two Flowers on the Same Branch: Qawmi and Alia Madrasas—Constructive Evaluation, Not Mutual Denigration

Two Flowers on the Same Branch: Qawmi and Alia Madrasas—Constructive Evaluation, Not Mutual Denigration

Recently, an increasingly confrontational and disparaging trend has become apparent among some scholars and educated circles associated with both the Qawmi and Alia educational traditions. This development raises serious questions about the health of the intellectual environment within Islamic education.

Some individuals from the Qawmi community, in particular, appear to suggest that the Alia system does not produce genuinely qualified Islamic scholars. Some have even gone so far as to claim that no one in this stream can recite the Qur’an correctly. Conversely, certain individuals from the Alia community make disparaging remarks about the Qawmi educational system and its contributions, seeking in various ways to belittle its scholars.

Such mutual denigration is conducive neither to healthy intellectual engagement nor to Islamic brotherhood or a constructive educational culture.

There is no denying that the overall standard of education in Alia madrasas currently falls short of expectations for various reasons. Concerns about the quality of Islamic and Arabic education in particular have persisted for a long time.

Nevertheless, it is also a historical fact that these institutions once produced many renowned Qur’an reciters, Islamic scholars, jurists, researchers, and educationists who made significant contributions to the country’s religious, educational, and social life. Even today, many Alia madrasa graduates go on to study at universities and other higher education institutions and make notable contributions nationally and internationally in education, research, administration, the judiciary, and various professions. It is therefore inconsistent with reality to dismiss the Alia educational system in its entirety.

The present condition of Alia education has multiple causes. Some are internal, including curricular shortcomings, educational quality, administrative weaknesses, and institutional limitations. Others arise from broader social, political, and policy-related circumstances.

Through articles, research-based writings, and sustained discussions on social media, I have, at various times, attempted to analyse these problems and highlight possible avenues for reform and improvement.

It is also important to recognise that not all Alia madrasas are alike. Some institutions continue to provide reasonably high-quality education through institutional or individual initiatives. They produce competent Qur’an reciters, qualified Islamic scholars, and talented students, although their numbers remain limited in relation to the overall need.

Another reality is that a considerable number of individuals with Qawmi backgrounds now obtain academic qualifications through the Alia and university systems and subsequently work in teaching, administration, and other professions. In recent years, employment opportunities have also emerged in some areas on the basis of Qawmi qualifications alone. This trend points to a positive aspect of interaction and cooperation between the two educational traditions.

At the same time, it must be unequivocally acknowledged that Qawmi madrasas have made a vital contribution to the foundations of Islamic and Arabic learning, Qur’anic recitation, memorisation of the Qur’an, and the preservation of traditional religious scholarship.

Every year, these institutions produce many skilled Qur’an reciters, *huffaz* (those who have memorised the Qur’an), and Islamic scholars. This is undoubtedly worthy of appreciation.

My own teaching and research experience has given me opportunities to work with students from the Qawmi tradition over many years. Based on these experiences, my observation is that the overall educational standards and academic environments of Qawmi madrasas are not uniformly satisfactory either.

Given that Qawmi institutions operate as a comprehensive and comparatively independent system of religious education, one might reasonably expect them to produce a proportionate number of outstanding researchers, scholars capable of *ijtihad*-oriented critical thinking, and intellectual leaders equipped to understand contemporary realities. In practice, however, the number of such scholars remains quite limited, whether or not this assessment is readily acknowledged.

The need for scholars who possess adequate knowledge of modern disciplines, contemporary intellectual trends, and global challenges is particularly acute today.

Nevertheless, the distinctive contribution of Qawmi madrasas to teaching correct Qur’anic recitation and preserving and developing traditional Islamic sciences deserves unequivocal recognition.

The reality, therefore, is that weaknesses and limitations exist, to varying degrees, in both educational traditions. Similarly, each has significant achievements, a rich heritage, and valuable contributions to its credit.

Consequently, belittling one another, showing contempt, or labelling an entire educational tradition as unqualified cannot constitute a fair or responsible position.

To describe Alia education in disparaging terms, to claim that no quality education is available there, or to assert that its students cannot recite the Qur’an correctly are sweeping generalisations divorced from reality and indicative of an attitude of unwarranted self-satisfaction.

Likewise, denying the historical contributions of Qawmi education, diminishing its achievements, or presenting it in a mocking tone is contrary to objectivity and reflects intellectual narrow-mindedness.

An objective assessment requires both traditions to identify their respective limitations honestly, undertake necessary reforms, and acknowledge one another’s positive contributions.

In this regard, it is worth remembering that Qawmi and Alia scholars once shared a rich tradition of mutual respect, cordial relations, and regular intellectual exchange. They sincerely appreciated one another’s knowledge, wisdom, and contributions.

I have personally witnessed this tradition as well. Several distinguished scholars among my own teachers were graduates of Darul Uloom Deoband, and I was fortunate to study under them. Their lives and work demonstrated how mutual respect, devotion to knowledge, and the prioritisation of broader religious interests could transcend differences of opinion. Their example remains worthy of emulation today.

If there is to be competition between the two traditions, it should be a competition to achieve excellence in knowledge, research, ethics, education, and service to society—not one characterised by mutual denigration and division.

Both Qawmi and Alia madrasas are integral parts of Bangladesh’s Islamic educational heritage. Their mutual cooperation, dialogue, and constructive self-criticism can contribute far more effectively to the overall advancement of Islamic education and the broader welfare of the nation than disparagement and division ever could.
